27) In Soviet literature, the words “matter,” “material,” “materialism,” and so on have unfortunately lost much of their clarity and precision.

Because of an unfortunate and unusual use of the term—although this usage goes back a long way, even to Marx—socialism, in its struggle against idealism, opposes it not with realism, as would normally be correct, but with materialism. Yet materialism ought properly to be opposed not to idealism but to spiritualism.

The doctrine of Marx-Lenin-Stalin is in fact not materialism at all. It is realism: the view that “being determines consciousness,” as opposed to idealism, which says that consciousness “determines” being.
What should properly be called materialism is the thoroughly absurd view that every kind of being is material—just as spiritualism is the equally absurd view that every kind of being is spiritual.
Marxism clearly has nothing to do with nonsense of this sort, which Engels called “philosophy for apothecaries.”

It is obviously absurd to claim that this table, the number five, War and Peace, the Soviet Constitution, a toothache, Chichikov, and the relation “being to the right of” all exist in exactly the same way—namely, “materially.”

Materialism must therefore do one of two things. Either it must defend absurdities of this kind, if it claims that everything is “material” and recognizes only one form of “matter”; or it must distinguish between different kinds of “material” existence.
But in the second case its materialism becomes little more than a play on words.

Instead of saying, for example, that iron is material while thought and will are immaterial, it will say that we are dealing with two completely different aspects of “matter,” irreducible to one another, and so on.
There is nothing inherently wrong with this, except that for the sake of clarity it is better to give different things different names.
Unfortunately, however, this misuse of the word “materialism” has had a damaging consequence.

On the one hand, once Marx’s realist doctrine had been labeled materialist, people began studying not only Marx himself but genuine materialists as well—that is, mediocre thinkers such as La Mettrie and Büchner.
On the other hand, after reading these materialists, people began criticizing them and then felt entitled to direct the same criticisms at Marx himself, even though Marx never shared their views.
And so we have reached the point where, to my own embarrassment, I have to justify in a footnote something as obvious as this: thought is not a property of material things simply as material things.

To avoid misunderstanding, then, I should emphasize that I use the word “matter” in its precise physical and scientific sense. I call “matter” precisely and only what can be measured in the CGS system—that is, in units of space (centimetres), weight (grams), and time (seconds).
Phenomena such as thought, will, freedom, and so on—in other words, precisely what is human in the human being—must obviously not be called “material.”
Nor should they be called “spiritual,” unless one simply means, as one should, that they exist in a very different way from the way things exist.
Unfortunately, even this terminology makes misunderstanding difficult to avoid.
Physics, for example, distinguishes “matter” from “energy.” Yet in my use of the term, physical energy is also “material,” since it too is measured in CGS units.
It might therefore be better to speak of “thinghood,” from the word “thing,” and then divide thinghood into “matter” and “energy.”
Phenomena that do not belong to thinghood—thought, will, and so on—could then be called “existentialities,” from the verb “to exist.”

We could speak, on the one hand, of the thing-like being of stones, trees, dogs, and so on, as well as of the human being insofar as he is an animal; and, on the other, of the existential being of the State, literature, science, and everything else that belongs specifically to the human in the human being.
But this unusual terminology would probably create new misunderstandings, since the words “existential” and “existentiality” are already used in other senses.
In particular, “existentiality” is ordinarily understood as referring to a “thing,” whereas I would want to oppose “existential” existence precisely to “thing-like” existence.

I do not know how to escape all these difficulties while preserving ordinary usage. So I will limit myself to protesting against the misuse of the word “matter” and its derivatives, such as “materialism.”
It would be interesting to replace the expression “dialectical and historical materialism” with “dialectical and historical realism.”
28) The word “atom” should be understood literally here: an indivisible particle possessing one and only one quality.
In present-day physics the atom is a complex system, and for that very reason its existence can of course come to an end.

Even the present-day electron is not an “atom” in the strict sense of the word, since it possesses two qualities: on the one hand weight and volume, and on the other charge and energy. For that reason it too can “die” and “be born,” passing from “matter”—the electron properly speaking—into energy—the proton—and back again.
But “matter” and “energy” are themselves eternal, insofar as each is something with one fixed and unchanging quality.
In Descartes, matter is eternal because it has only one quality, extension, just as the soul is eternal because it possesses only one quality, thought.

My argument may seem completely wrong, since things do in certain respects depend on the external conditions with which they interact. But this objection rests on a misunderstanding.
I am speaking here about essential qualities, or “attributes,” not contingent qualities, or “accidents.”
A horse, for example, may be piebald or palomino. That simply means that the color of its coat does not enter into its logical concept.
By contrast, a feature such as “having four legs,” let us say, does enter into its definition.

Suppose, in accordance with evolutionary theory, that the animal we now call a horse were to develop into a two-legged animal. This is possible. But in that case it would cease to be—and cease to be called—a horse. It would be a different animal.
The situation is exactly the same as when an “atom” of helium is transformed into an “atom” of hydrogen. It then ceases to be a helium atom and becomes a hydrogen atom.
But hydrogen and helium, taken in themselves, have unchanging qualities that depend only on what they themselves are.
So the question is this: should the human being be understood in the same way as such an atom?
Should we attribute “essential qualities” to human beings? Or should we suppose that a human being can change his very essence while still remaining human?
Hegel correctly answers yes to the second possibility.
The one “essential and constant quality” of the human being is precisely the capacity to change his own “essential” qualities.
But this will become clear only later.
